final.title: Recover brittle automation by naming the one workflow
final.body:
When automation gets brittle, don’t start by rebuilding the whole stack. Start with one broken workflow and one simple question: what failed, and what is that failure costing you in time or errors right now?

That gives you a bounded decision. You stop talking about “AI” in general and compare three practical options on one recurring workflow: fix the automation, replace it, or keep it manual for now. For an owner-operator, that is the real choice. The build stays technical; the decision stays human.

Next, check whether the workflow is even a fit. Is it repetitive, measurable, and stable enough to benefit from automation? If not, the honest answer may be process cleanup or a clearer manual handoff. Not every broken script deserves a comeback tour.

The practical next step is a short diagnostic: name the one workflow, locate where it fails, and decide whether AI fits before you spend time rebuilding it. If it does fit, the next discussion is pilot scope and fixed cost, with final approval still in the owner’s hands. No autonomous money movement, no hidden handoffs, no pretending the machine gets the last word.

final.title: When brittle automation breaks, start with one workflow
final.body:
If automation has gone brittle, do not start by rebuilding the whole stack. Start with one question: which recurring manual workflow failed when the automation broke, and what is that failure costing you in time or errors right now?

That narrows the decision. You are no longer debating “AI” in general; you are comparing a small set of options on one workflow: fix the automation, replace it, or leave it manual for now. For a small business owner, that is the real choice. The build stays technical; the decision stays human.

Then check fit. Is the workflow repetitive, measurable, and stable enough to benefit from automation at all? If not, the honest answer may be process cleanup or a clearer handoff, not another layer of scripts. Some workflows are simply not worth rescuing with more automation, which is inconvenient but useful.

The next step is practical: name the one workflow, note where it fails, and decide whether AI fits before you spend time rebuilding it. If it does fit, the follow-up is a short diagnostic to define pilot scope, fixed cost, and measures, with the owner keeping final approval. No autonomous money movement. No hidden handoffs. Just a bounded decision.
